assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clear case of a tool that opens a door: correcting spherical aberration made routine sub-angstrom imaging and spectroscopy of atoms, interfaces and defects possible, and it now underpins materials physics, catalysis, 2D materials and quantum-device characterisation. It is an invention that was experimentally demonstrated, then adopted worldwide.
assessment.attribution: Rose supplied the theoretical design of the correctors, Haider led the realisation of the hexapole corrector for TEM, and Urban led the demonstration and application to atomic-resolution imaging. This maps naturally onto three people. Other contributors, notably Krivanek for the STEM corrector, are not in the credited list, so I cannot propose them here and the credit question is not fully resolved.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of independent confirmation and commercial adoption on all major instrument platforms; recognition is, if anything, overdue. Earlier microscopy prizes (Ruska 1986) set a precedent for recognising electron optics.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept a corrector prize without the STEM-side originators.
My own field proximity: I would want colleagues to test whether my judgement here is balanced rather than parochial.
Priority between TEM and STEM corrector developments is something I would check against the historical record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength optical lattice proposal and its demonstration made neutral-atom clocks with fractional uncertainty around 1e-18 possible. This is a genuine invention with measurable benefit: redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and searches for dark matter.
assessment.attribution: Katori originated the optical lattice clock concept and first demonstrated it; Ye led the realisation of the highest-performance lattice clocks and many precision-metrology advances. A two-person prize is clean. Related ion-clock work (not credited here) and the earlier comb work already honoured in 2005 limit overlap concerns.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce and surpass the performance; international metrology bodies are moving toward a redefinition of the second. Timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and with the 2012 prize for ion control may be raised.
Credit for early lattice-clock work by other groups (for example Sr clocks at other institutes) is not captured in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of flat bands at the magic angle followed by experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform, moire quantum matter, that was not accessible before. Original, striking and rapidly generalised to other moire systems.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the original experimental discovery. This is a good theory-plus-experiment configuration, though the 2018 experiments were co-authored by many (including Cao and others) and other theory (for example earlier flat-band work) may have claims.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups; mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, but the discovery itself is solid. Possibly slightly early, but the field is mature enough.
uncertainties: The superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved, so the interpretation is not fully stable.
Credit to early-career experimentalists and earlier theoretical work on twisted bilayers is an open allocation question.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for a technological outcome.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators represent a conceptual and experimental shift in understanding electronic states, with HgTe quantum wells giving the first experimental realisation. Lasting impact on topological materials and spintronics.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposal and Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group made the original experimental observation in HgTe (after Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal, who are not in this entry's credited list). Zhang's death and the credit for the HgTe proposal complicate a fair configuration. The three credited names are a coherent triple for this entry.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed in many materials, including three-dimensional topological insulators; mature and stable.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe prediction is absent from the credited names and needs priority checking.
The overlap with the topological-phase prize in 2016 may weigh against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature giant tunnel magnetoresistance in crystalline MgO junctions made magnetic read heads and MRAM practical. The result is an experimental discovery followed by large technological and societal impact, in the line of the 2007 GMR prize.
assessment.attribution: Yuasa and Parkin independently reported the large room-temperature effect in 2004 in the same period, which is the original experimental work. Butler's earlier theoretical prediction of coherent tunnelling is credited here; I would not exclude him, but two experimentalists is the cleaner story. Independent simultaneous discovery is a fair-credit argument rather than a problem.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of replication and commercial deployment. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether Butler (theory) should replace or join one of the experimentalists.
Fairness to the Japanese and US groups, and to Jaffres and Moodera work on earlier TMR, who are not credited here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2007 Lorimer burst was an original discovery of a new class of astrophysical transient, now thousands of fast radio bursts, with uses as probes of the intergalactic medium. This is an original observation that opened a new window.
assessment.attribution: Lorimer, McLaughlin and Bailes led the discovery paper, which is a good fit for a three-person prize, but the 2007 burst was found in archival data and the discoveries of repeaters and the Galactic burst from SGR 1935 involve other groups (CHIME, others).
assessment.maturity: Verified, but the physical origin remains unresolved, and the interpretation (magnetars? other sources?) is still evolving. The discovery stands even if the mechanism is open.
uncertainties: Origin of FRBs is undetermined, which some members will say makes the prize premature.
Credit for the first confirmation (Keane, Thornton et al.) and the repeater finding is not covered by the credited names.
Not an issue of a single decisive laureate group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the 2017 TXS 0506+056 association established neutrino astronomy with a cubic-kilometre detector buried in ice, an instrument achievement and a discovery. Strong 'new window' appeal.
assessment.attribution: Halzen drove the concept and the collaboration; Karle was central to the detector construction and the analysis. Spiering's contribution is more tied to pioneering neutrino telescopes (Baikal, Lake and ice). A large collaboration makes a limited-person prize inherently imperfect, and I would want careful verification of who did the original work.
assessment.maturity: Observation is solid at more than 5 sigma and independent of other detectors, but source identification is still thin. The first discovery is mature; astronomy is early.
uncertainties: Large collaboration with many essential contributors beyond three credited names.
Whether credit should go to the Baikal and AMANDA pioneers.
Few identified sources so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography is a direct, measurable benefit to humanity, with micrometre-resolution retinal imaging that is standard care in ophthalmology. It is an instrument invention with an optical-physics origin (low-coherence interferometry).
assessment.attribution: The 1991 Science paper by Huang, Swanson, Fujimoto and colleagues is the key original demonstration, with Fujimoto as group leader. Prior work on low-coherence interferometry in the eye (Fercher and others) and later Fourier-domain advances raise a priority question that I would investigate carefully. Whether the physics prize or medicine is the right home is also a question.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and clinically adopted for over two decades. Timely.
uncertainties: Prior low-coherence work (Fercher, Hitzenberger, Youngquist) may undercut the originality of the 1991 invention.
Fit with the physics prize rather than physiology or medicine.
Fair split among three credited names versus the first author contributions.
